newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - January 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - January 31.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- TV BROADCASTERS LINK UP IN BID FOR DIGITAL SERVICE

A powerful consortium has been formed by UK broadcasters to bid for the right to launch digital terrestrial television in Britain. The group, to be known as British Digital Broadcasting, comprises satellite broadcaster BSkyB and terrestrial groups Carlton Communications and Granada Group. In what could be one of the biggest shake-ups in British broadcasting, the group is also thought to have secured agreement with the BBC to broadcast up to eight subscription channels.
-- PREMIER FARNELL PUTS BLAME ON BZW

Howard Poulson, chief executive of Anglo-US electronic components group Premier Farnell, blamed the company's broker BZW for Wednesday's controversial profits warning. Poulson described the warning as "unnecessary", and revealed that BZW changed its mind over the issue after originally advising that a warning was not needed. The warning, that profits would fall up to 8 percent below expectations, prompted a 25 percent fall in Farnell's share price.
-- DTI ASKED TO QUIZ WILLIAM COOK ON TRADING FORECASTS

A request has been lodged with the DTI to investigate alleged discrepancies between a downbeat trading statement issued by steel castings group William Cook, and financial information it gave to its bankers one month previously. The move comes as the group's chief executive, Andrew Cook, is canvassing support for a proposed 79.5 million stg MBO. Cook suggested that the request is an attempt by rival castings group Triplex Lloyd, which has bid 71.8 million stg for William Cook, to "destabilise our defence and the buy-out offer".
-- BRUSSELS IN MOVE TO BREAK AIR SLOT DEADLOCK

The European Commission is thought to be set to offer a compromise solution for the dispute over airport take-off and landing slots. EU Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock is understood to favour creating a market in which the slots can legally be bought and sold. At present, slots are granted in perpetuity but are trading on a "grey market". EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert is thought to oppose legalising the sales. The proposed compromise would allow some trading, but of slots which would have limited life spans.
-- COURT FREES NADIR AIDE FROM FIVE-YEAR SENTENCE

The Court of Appeal has ruled that a five-year jail sentence imposed on a former aide to fugitive businessman Asil Nadir was "disproportionate", and granted the woman immediate bail. The ruling effectively quashes the sentence imposed on Elizabeth Forsyth, the former personal banker to Nadir, who was convicted on charges of handling stolen money.
-- TOYOTA CHIEF ACTS TO CALM EMU ROW

Hiroshi Okuda, the president of Japanese automotive giant Toyota who on Wednesday suggested that the company would reconsider its European investment strategy if the UK stayed out of European monetary union, has sought to calm the political row sparked by his comments. Toyota employs 2,500 people at an assembly plant in the UK, and the comments were seized on by the Labour party as evidence of the damage the government's wait-and-see approach to the EMU is causing. Okuda has since softened his earlier warning, but maintained that the EMU will still influence decisions on which countries the company will invest in.
-- POWER UTILITY TO SHAKE UP SHARES

Kent-based power company Southern Electric is reported to be considering a share restructuring, with an announcement possible as early as Friday. The move, which could see about 200 million stg being returned to shareholders, would follow a similar scheme unveiled by Yorkshire Water on Thursday in which the Leeds-based utility will pay 147 million stg back to shareholders in a share split and 9-for-10 consolidation.
-- GLAXO TO AXE NON-EXECUTIVE CHAIRMAN POST

Pharmaceuticals giant Glaxo Wellcome has announced a reshuffle of top management in which the post of non-executive chairman has been abolished. Under the changes, Sir Richard Skyes moves from chief executive and deputy chairman to executive chairman, while current managing director Sean Lance will replace Skyes. The move to axe the non-executive chairman post represents a break with what many fund managers regard as best practice in corporate governance.
-- ALCATEL SHARES RISE 15 PERCENT AS RECOVERY PLAN SHOWS RESULTS

Shares in French engineering and telecoms group Alcatel Alsthom rose 15 percent on the Paris stock exchange on Thursday as the company indicated positive results from the recovery plan it launched in 1995. Alcatel said it expected operating income in 1996 to exceed FFr2.7bn (300m stg), more than four times the comparable figure for 1995. Analyst Angela Dean of Morgan Stanley in London said the results showed Alcatel was benefiting from repositioning its core telecoms business in fast-growing areas such as mobile telephony and transmissions.
-- GULF ATTACKS CLYDE FORECASTS

Canadian oil and gas group Gulf Canada Resouces, which has tabled a 432 million stg hostile takeover bid for UK oil independent Clyde Petroleum, has attacked the "unrealistic production forecasts" issued by its bid target. Gulf has seized on estimates for an oilfield bought by Clyde two days before the bid was launched in December. The Canadian predator has drawn on research commissioned from an independent consultant to dismiss Clyde's calculations for the field as "overly optimistic".
